name: Manage claims and disputes
summary: When a change price cannot be agreed, a project is delayed by events the owner is responsible for, or a trade claims against the company, the claims manager turns the dispute into a documented claim. The project team assembles records, a scheduler analyses the delay, the claims manager prices and writes the claim, and the general counsel approves it, negotiates it, takes it to mediation and, if needed, to arbitration or court. Claims are slow because records are scattered across systems, schedulers and project managers are busy on live work, owners take months to respond and formal disputes last more than a year.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian national general contractor with a small in-house legal and claims group supporting about 220 active building projects.
baseline.notes: Contracts are mostly CCDC 2 and CCDC 5 with Part 8 negotiation, mediation and arbitration; external counsel and experts are retained for formal disputes.

trigger: An operations manager refers a disputed change, a delay notice or a subcontractor's claim against the company to the claims manager.
end_state: The claim is settled and recorded as a change order, decided by an award or judgment and recorded, or dropped.

volume.seasonality: More referrals near substantial performance and in the first quarter, when closeout accounts are settled.

evidence.note: Organisation file estimate (about 48 claims a year across 220 projects). Kept unchanged.
Prepares, negotiates and manages claims; FTE is the author's estimate (most of 4 claims managers). Loaded cost from the organisation file (salaried wage x 1.35).
Records, review and negotiation support; FTE is the author's estimate. Loaded cost from the organisation file (salaried wage x 1.35).

systems.name: Project management platform (drawings, RFIs, submittals, daily logs, change events)
Construction ERP (job cost, general ledger, payables, receivables, payroll)
Reporting and dashboards (Excel cost reports, Power BI)
CPM scheduling software (Primavera P6, Microsoft Project)

steps.name: Open the claim file
steps.description: The claims manager receives a referral from an operations manager (a disputed change, a delay notice or a trade's claim against the company), opens a matter file, sets up a folder in the document system and records the contract, owner, amounts and notice dates.
inputs: disputed change, delay notice or trade claim

evidence.note: Claims managers carry several matters each and new referrals wait; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Assess merit and notice compliance
steps.description: The claims manager reads the contract, the change and delay notices, correspondence and the consultant's findings to judge whether the company has entitlement, whether contract notice time limits were met and roughly what the claim is worth. Weak claims go back to the project for a commercial settlement.

evidence.note: Failure to understand or comply with contract obligations is the leading cause of North American disputes; share not pursued is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Review the legal position
steps.description: Contracts counsel reviews the merit assessment against the contract terms, supplementary conditions, notice provisions and dispute clauses, and advises on time limits for dispute notices, mediation and arbitration or court action.

evidence.note: CCDC Part 8 notice, negotiation, mediation and arbitration steps and time limits.

steps.name: Travel to site and interview the team
steps.description: The claims manager travels to the project, walks the work with the superintendent and interviews the project manager, superintendent and engineers about what happened and when. Out-of-region projects need a flight and an overnight stay.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the company works in Ontario, Western and Atlantic Canada.

steps.name: Assemble project records
steps.description: The project manager and site team pull daily reports, RFIs, submittal logs, change logs, meeting minutes, photos and correspondence for the claim period into the claim folder. Missing or inconsistent records weaken the claim.

error.defect_description: Records incomplete or contemporaneous notice missing.

evidence.note: Project managers do this alongside running live projects; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Extract cost records
steps.description: The project accountant runs job cost reports from the ERP for the claim period by cost code, with labour hours, equipment charges, subcontract payments and site overheads. They reconcile the extracts to the general ledger.

error.defect_description: Costs coded to the wrong period or code.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Analyse the delay
steps.description: The scheduler compares the baseline schedule with each monthly update and the as-built dates, runs a windows analysis to find which events drove the critical path, and allocates delay between owner, contractor and neutral causes.

evidence.note: Twelve schedulers support all projects, so claim work queues; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Quantify the claim
steps.description: The claims manager prices the claim: extended site overheads, extended equipment and crane time, labour productivity loss, escalation, subcontractor pass-through claims and financing, tying each head of claim to the records and delay analysis.

next.condition: large or complex; external expert needed

evidence.note: Average North American dispute value $37.9 million in 2020, which drives expert use on large claims; the 25% share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Retain an external expert
steps.description: For large claims the claims manager obtains approval to retain a forensic scheduling or quantum expert, agrees scope and fees, and sends the record set.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for the expert report
steps.description: The expert reviews the records and schedules, asks questions and issues a report on delay and quantum. The report is often the critical path of the claim.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Draft the claim submission
steps.description: The claims manager writes the claim document: narrative of events, contract entitlement, delay analysis, quantum and appendices of records. The submission is written to stand on its own before the consultant and, later, a mediator or arbitrator.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Project team reviews the draft
steps.description: The project manager checks facts, dates and quantities in the draft and flags anything that would weaken the relationship with the owner on the live project. Corrections go back to the claims manager.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve the claim submission
steps.description: The general counsel approves the claim for submission after weighing value, cost to pursue, owner relationship and future bidding with that owner. Large claims are discussed with the chief operating officer.

control.basis: Company delegation of authority for claims and litigation

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Submit the claim
steps.description: The claims manager issues the claim to the consultant and owner as the contract requires, by courier or email, and diarises the response and dispute notice deadlines.

control.basis: Prime contract notice provisions (CCDC 2 Part 8 and GC 6.6)

evidence.note: Consultant makes findings on claims; disputes follow Part 8.

steps.name: Wait for the consultant's finding and owner response
steps.description: The consultant reviews the claim and issues a finding, and the owner responds, often with its own consultant's analysis. Detailed claims get extra time for findings.

evidence.note: GC 6.6.5 allows more time for findings on detailed claims; durations are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Answer requests for particulars
steps.description: The claims manager answers the owner's or consultant's questions and document requests, often with more cost backup or schedule runs, and resubmits.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Negotiate with the owner
steps.description: The claims manager and project manager meet the owner and consultant over several sessions to narrow the issues and trade heads of claim, often packaging the claim with open change orders and the closeout account.

evidence.note: Most North American disputes were settled by party-to-party negotiation in 2020; shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for a mediation date
steps.description: The parties agree on a mediator under the contract's dispute clause and find a date that suits the mediator, counsel and executives on both sides.

control.basis: CCDC 2 Part 8: negotiation and mediation before arbitration

evidence.note: Project Mediator appointed under Part 8; waits are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Prepare the mediation brief
steps.description: The claims manager prepares the mediation brief and settlement ranges with contracts counsel and briefs the general counsel and operations leadership on walk-away positions.

error.defect_description: Settlement authority not agreed in advance.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Attend the mediation
steps.description: The general counsel leads the company's team at a one- or two-day mediation with the owner, the mediator and counsel, and decides whether to accept the settlement on offer.

evidence.note: Mediation is non-binding and without prejudice; success share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Decide on arbitration or litigation
steps.description: The general counsel weighs cost, likely outcome, time and the owner relationship and decides whether to refer the dispute to arbitration or court, or settle at the owner's last figure. The referral has a short deadline after mediation ends.

control.basis: CCDC 2 Part 8: referral to arbitration within 10 Working Days after mediation ends

evidence.note: Part 8 referral period; shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Run the arbitration or action with external counsel
steps.description: The claims manager instructs external counsel, assembles document productions, prepares witness statements with the project team and works with experts through pleadings, discoveries and hearing preparation.

evidence.note: North American disputes averaged 17.6 months to resolve in 2019; the effort range is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for the hearing and award
steps.description: The arbitrator or court schedules the hearing, hears the evidence and issues an award or judgment. Many cases settle on the eve of the hearing.

evidence.note: Average North American dispute length 17.6 months (2019) and 14.2 months (2020) for the whole dispute; the hearing wait range and settlement share are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Assess the award
steps.description: The general counsel reviews the award or judgment with external counsel, decides whether to appeal or seek review, and instructs payment or collection.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve the settlement
steps.description: The general counsel approves the settlement terms within delegated authority, with the chief financial officer for large amounts, checking the effect on the project forecast and any trade pass-through obligations.

control.basis: Company delegation of authority for claim settlements

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Document the settlement
steps.description: The claims manager drafts or checks the settlement agreement and release, and asks the project team to have the consultant issue a change order for the agreed amount and time so it can be billed.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Record the settlement in the ERP
steps.description: The project accountant records the settlement in the ERP contract value and updates the project forecast, reversing any claim revenue that was recognised above the settled amount.

error.defect_description: Revenue adjustment posted to the wrong period.

control.basis: IFRS 15 variable consideration: claim revenue recognised only when highly probable; external audit review of claims

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Record the award in the ERP
steps.description: The project accountant records the award or judgment amount, interest and costs in the ERP and updates the project forecast and receivables.

control.basis: IFRS 15 variable consideration and external audit review of claims

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: External expert retained
exceptions.description: Large or complex claims wait one to three months for a forensic scheduling or quantum expert report.

exceptions.name: Mediation
exceptions.description: Negotiation reaches an impasse and the parties go to a one- or two-day mediation under the contract's dispute clause.

exceptions.name: Arbitration or litigation
exceptions.description: Mediation fails and the dispute is referred to arbitration or court, adding a year or more.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from referral to settlement, award or withdrawal
benchmarks.population: All claims referred to the claims group of a Canadian building contractor, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate. Arcadis reports average North American dispute lengths of 14.2 to 17.6 months, but for formal disputes averaging $18.8 to $37.9 million; most claims here are smaller and settle by negotiation, so the median is set lower and the 90th percentile (about 16 months) near the Arcadis average.

benchmarks.population: North American construction disputes in the Arcadis Global Construction Disputes Reports
North American construction disputes in the Arcadis Global Construction Disputes Reports

pain_points.description: Records for the claim period are scattered across the project platform, email and the ERP and have to be pulled by busy project staff.

evidence.note: Author's observation of common practice.

pain_points.description: Owners and consultants take months to respond and ask for more particulars.

evidence.note: GC 6.6.5 allows extra time for findings on detailed claims.

pain_points.description: Formal disputes take more than a year.

evidence.note: Average North American dispute length 14.2 to 17.6 months.

pain_points.description: Failure to give contract notices on time weakens or bars claims.

sources.title: Report: Cost and length of North American construction disputes increased in 2019
sources.supports: North America: average dispute value rose from $16.3 million (2018) to $18.8 million (2019); average time to resolve rose from 15.2 to 17.6 months; top cause a contractor or subcontractor failing to understand or comply with contractual obligations.

sources.title: Cost of construction disputes increased dramatically in 2020 (Arcadis Global Construction Disputes Report 2021 news release)
sources.supports: North America: average dispute value rose from $18.8 million (2019) to $37.9 million (2020); average length shortened from 17.6 to 14.2 months; leading causes failure to understand or comply with contract obligations, owner-directed changes, third-party or force majeure changes; most disputes settled by party-to-party negotiation.

sources.title: Construction Industry Disputes: Use Of Negotiation, Mediation And Arbitration Clause
sources.publisher: Goldman Sloan Nash & Haber LLP (via Legal 500 / Mondaq)
sources.supports: CCDC Part 8: a party may refer a dispute to the Consultant for a written finding; notice of dispute within 15 Working Days of the finding, reply within 10 Working Days; amicable negotiation; Project Mediator appointed within 20 Working Days of award; mediation non-binding; if mediation fails either party may refer the dispute to arbitration within 10 Working Days; litigation remains if the parties do not agree to arbitrate.

sources.title: Practice Tip PT.23.11: CCDC 2-2020 Stipulated Price Contract, Overview of the Changes in the 2020 Version and Recommended Supplementary Conditions
sources.supports: CCDC 2-2020 GC 6.3.7: change directive costs apply in as much as they contribute directly to implementing the change directive; GC 8.2 adjudication added to align with the Construction Act; negotiation-mediation-arbitration dispute procedure; Consultant must make findings on claims for a change in Contract Price regardless of size or number (GC 2.2.11); GC 6.6.5 allows more time for findings on detailed claims.

assumptions: Unit of work is one claim referred to the claims group; change disputes settled by the project team before referral stay in gc-ops-change-order.
Trade claims against the company are included because the claims manager handles them; the organisation file only lists owner-side triggers.
External counsel and experts are outside parties; their time is modelled as waits, and their fees are not in the labour cost.
The claims manager's travel to out-of-region sites uses commercial flights and rental cars, so no company resource is tied up.
Claim revenue recognition follows IFRS 15 as reported by a TSX-listed contractor.
Waits include nights and weekends; legal and project office roles work weekdays.

The simulated 90th percentile (about 390 days) is below the 480-day benchmark because only about 7% of claims reach arbitration or court in this model; the Arcadis averages describe large formal disputes, which are a minority of this contractor's claims.
